extracted.intended_audience: administrative-law scholars, agency counsel, judges, and regulatory practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Legal and practical standards for agency notice-and-comment rulemaking, especially the agency’s duty to consider and respond to public comments and related procedural doctrines (standing, materiality, interim rules, reviewability). Targeted to readers working on or litigating federal rulemaking under the APA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency duty to respond to rulemaking comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies have a duty to respond to rulemaking comments — a duty the Supreme Court expressly recognized (e.g., Mortgage Bankers) and that has become a settled feature of administrative practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement of this duty ensures agencies give comments enough attention to reply to significant arguments; courts review those responses under normal standards of reasoned decisionmaking. Agencies typically implement the duty in preambles to final rules; courts expect substantive engagement rather than perfunctory acknowledgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA § 553(c) 'consideration of the relevant matter presented' / concise general statement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: APA § 553(c) requires that after consideration of relevant matters presented during the comment period, the agency incorporate in the rules adopted a concise general statement of their basis and purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts rely on the concise general statement to see what major policy issues were ventilated and why the agency reacted as it did. Mere boilerplate or a mere note that a comment 'mentioned' an authority will often be inadequate for review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materiality / significance threshold for comments
rubrics_metrics.description: A court asks whether a comment was material/significant enough that the agency needed to address it — framed in some writings as whether it was possible the comment 'might' have changed the agency’s mind, but that framing sets a low bar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A preferable framing for review is whether the agency could reasonably have failed to take account of the comment. This asks whether it was reasonable for the agency to ignore the point rather than relying on a speculative 'might' standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble content: must 'come to grips' with issues raised (collective responses permitted)
rubrics_metrics.description: The preamble to a final rule must grapple with issues raised in comments; it need not identify each commenter and may respond collectively to issues raised in multiple comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts focus on whether the substance of the agency’s response is cogent and sufficient for review. Collective or aggregated responses are acceptable where individual identification would be impractical, so long as the agency addresses the significant arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies are not required to individually read identical or nearly identical comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Because rulemakings sometimes receive hundreds of thousands or millions of electronically submitted identical or nearly identical comments, APA § 553(c)’s implication of individualized consideration has been recognized as impractical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACUS and practice accept the use of sorting software and managerial procedures; agencies need not ensure a person reads each duplicate comment, though they must address significant substantive arguments that emerge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue exhaustion in rulemaking/judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: A judicial-review litigant may not rely on an issue not raised at the agency level unless it was raised by any commenter (or obvious enough that the agency should have raised it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issue exhaustion does not require that the particular plaintiff raised the issue; if any commenter or the agency raised it, a later litigant may rely on it in court. This preserves access to judicial review even for litigants who did not themselves comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing limits for procedural challenges (Lujan / Summers / 'in vacuo')
rubrics_metrics.description: To have Article III standing, a plaintiff must show a concrete, particularized, and imminent injury in fact; an allegation of a procedural violation alone is generally insufficient unless accompanied by a concrete injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summers v. Earth Island Institute held that deprivation of a procedural right 'in vacuo' is insufficient. Thus, an alleged breach of the duty to respond to comments will usually not confer standing absent a tangible injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possibility of informational standing by statute
rubrics_metrics.description: Where statutes create legal information rights, courts have allowed suits to obtain information (e.g., FOIA, campaign-finance disclosures); by analogy, standing to vindicate a duty to respond could be conceived if the duty were recast as an individual right to receive responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reconceptualization is theoretically possible but fraught: granting individual rights to responses risks ossification of rulemaking and would be a significant departure from current norms. Courts have been skeptical about transforming the duty to respond into an enforceable individual right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review standard: responses judged for reasoned decisionmaking / arbitrariness
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts review agencies’ responses to comments under ordinary standards of reasoned decisionmaking (arbitrary-and-capricious review) and expect the agency’s rationale to be accessible from the administrative record and preamble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'concise general statement' must enable judicial review of the agency’s reasoning; superficial treatment of significant arguments can lead to remand or invalidation (cases cited: Portland Cement, Nova Scotia Food Prods., etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interim (interim-final) rules, good-cause findings, and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: When agencies issue interim rules under good-cause exceptions, courts may later find the good-cause finding erroneous; agencies remain accountable for harms the rule produced before the APA violation was cured through post-promulgation procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an interim rule goes into effect but is later invalidated, persons who violated a rule before the agency cured it should not be penalized. Enforcement of the duty to respond to post-promulgation comments can mitigate policy concerns about haste in interim rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-promulgation comments and agency responses
rubrics_metrics.description: When agencies solicit or receive comments after promulgating an interim rule, they retain the duty to respond to significant comments submitted post-promulgation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts can review those responses; acknowledging and responding conscientiously to post-promulgation comments strengthens the agency’s position in litigation (Little Sisters example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding perfunctory engagement — 'noting merely' is inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply noting that a comment 'mentioned' a point or authority without analyzing its arguments is insufficient; courts have invalidated rules where agency responses were merely perfunctory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must do more than cursorily record that comments existed; they must analyze and explain their reasons for accepting or rejecting substantial arguments (see La. Fed. Land Bank and related authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulemaking serves collective public goals; not designed to guarantee individualized due process
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice-and-comment procedure is best understood as a set of agency duties to the public at large to promote collective values like accuracy and political accountability, not a mechanism guaranteeing individual fairness in each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bi‑Metallic and subsequent doctrine reflect that due-process protections that apply in adjudication typically do not extend to rulemaking; courts therefore treat rulemaking as impersonal and focused on general lawfulness and reasonableness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative burden and ossification concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring expansive, highly individualized responses or converting the duty to respond into an enforceable individual right could substantially increase agency workload and contribute to ossification of the administrative process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and commentators acknowledge these costs; agencies, ACUS, and commentators have sought pragmatic solutions (e.g., collective responses, software-assisted sorting) that balance fairness and administrative feasibility.
